title: PM2.5-glucose coupling varies with diabetes severity
statement: PM2.5-glucose coupling (zero-lag correlation and peak cross-correlation) differs across diabetes severity groups, suggesting environmental pollutant exposure modulates glycemic dynamics in a severity-dependent manner.
mechanism: PM2.5 exposure triggers systemic inflammation and oxidative stress, which impairs insulin signaling and promotes hepatic glucose output. In healthy individuals, homeostatic mechanisms buffer these effects, maintaining weak PM2.5-glucose coupling. As diabetes progresses and homeostatic reserves diminish, the glucose system becomes more sensitive to environmental perturbations, potentially amplifying PM2.5-glucose coupling. Alternatively, PM2.5 may differentially affect autonomic tone, indirectly modulating glucose dynamics.
predictions: PM2.5-glucose zero-lag correlation differs across diabetes severity groups
PM2.5-glucose peak cross-correlation amplitude increases with severity
PM2.5-HR coupling may also show severity-dependent differences

literature.title: Air pollution and diabetes association
literature.key_finding: PM2.5 exposure is associated with increased diabetes incidence and worsened glycemic control.
literature.relevance: Epidemiological basis for PM2.5-glucose coupling hypothesis.

feasibility.statistical_power: Marginal for small effects (d~0.16) given environmental data noise
key_challenges: PM2.5 data is spatially interpolated, not personal exposure
Temporal resolution mismatch between environmental and physiological data
Multiple testing across coupling metrics and environmental variables
dataset_limitations: PM2.5 is ambient (outdoor), not personal exposure
Short 10-day window may not capture sufficient PM2.5 variability

test_plan.primary_method: Kruskal-Wallis test for PM2.5-glucose coupling features across severity groups with FDR correction
implementation_steps: Align PM2.5 hourly data with CGM and HR streams
Compute zero-lag correlation and peak cross-correlation between PM2.5 and glucose per person
Test for group differences across severity
test_plan.success_criterion: FDR-significant PM2.5-glucose coupling differences across severity groups with consistent direction
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No significant differences, or effects driven by site/season confounding
secondary_methods: Cross-correlation function analysis at multiple lags

sensitivity_checks.name: PM2.5-HR coupling metrics
sensitivity_checks.details: Mostly null — no consistent PM2.5-HR coupling differences

results.interpretation: Weak signal for PM2.5-glucose zero-lag coupling differing by severity (FDR=0.014, d=0.164), but peak cross-correlation is not significant (FDR=0.080) and PM2.5-HR coupling is largely null. The signal is too weak and inconsistent to draw firm conclusions about environmental modulation of glycemic coupling.
results.surprises: PM2.5-HR coupling was mostly null, whereas PM2.5-glucose showed a borderline signal. Environmental modulation may be glucose-specific rather than systemic.

issues: Ambient PM2.5 is a poor proxy for personal exposure
Site confounding may drive the signal
Borderline significance even for the primary metric
suggestions: Need personal PM2.5 exposure monitors for stronger test
Require more rigorous time-series controls (e.g., surrogate data testing)
Consider temperature and humidity as alternative environmental drivers

notes: Weak signal that needs stronger time-series controls before causal claims. PM2.5 data quality (ambient, not personal) is a major limitation.
